activity: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
knowledge_domain: to calculate the resistance of a wire from measured voltage and current using Ohm's law
fact: Current measured in milliamps must be changed into amps before using Ohm's law; 250 milliamps is 0.25 amps.
story:
The kitchen table had become a lab. Alexia laid out the battery pack, the multimeter, and a coil of thin copper wire, then smoothed her notebook page where she had written her plan. Fletcher had texted her the setup an hour ago: measure the voltage across the wire, measure the current through it, divide one by the other, and you had the resistance. She could smell the faint warm-plastic odor of the battery pack as she clipped the probes in place.

The multimeter showed 3.0 volts for the voltage, which seemed sensible. Then she switched the dial to read current, and the display flickered and settled on 250. She wrote it down, did the division, and frowned. Three divided by 250 gave her 0.012. That could not be right. A wire with almost no resistance would behave like a dead short, and the battery pack would have gotten hot, but it sat there cool and quiet under the lamp. She pressed her palm against it just to be sure. Nothing.

She texted Fletcher, then sat back and looked at the numbers. The voltage part she trusted; the needle on the meter had been steady. What she could not see was the thing she was actually hunting for. Resistance was invisible, hiding somewhere in that opaque red plastic casing of the wire spool, and she could only infer it from the two numbers on the screen. So if the answer looked wrong, one of the numbers had to be lying. She ran her finger over her notebook and stopped at the 250. Next to the digits, half hidden by her thumb, was a tiny label on the meter's screen: mA. Milliamps. Fletcher's voice, from last week's class, surfaced in her memory: he had emphasized checking units before recording anything, and she had rolled her eyes at him.

She checked the meter again, then rummaged in her backpack for the sheet from Ms. Goh's class. Milliamps had to become amps first. So her reading was not 250 amps, it was 0.25 amps. She erased the old answer, did the division again, and got 12. Ohm's law had been working the whole time; her wire was fine, and the tiny difference in units had shrunk her answer a thousandfold. The twist was that she had spent ten minutes suspecting the copper coil when the real culprit was her own handwriting.

There was a knock at the back door. Ms. Goh stood there holding a plate of cookies, and her eyes went straight to the tangle of wire. "Homework?" she asked. Alexia held up the notebook, tapped the circled 12, and said, "I caught the milliamps before they caught me."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: In their 1999 dual process model, researchers Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut described grieving people as moving back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life.
story:
Eve stood between her parents at the edge of the grass, holding a bundle of daisies because her grandmother had a bias toward daisies over roses, always saying roses were for people who wanted to be looked at. The cemetery was quiet except for a wind chime on a stake two rows over, the kind with paper notes hanging from it that read things like Miss your laugh. The pastor said the last words, and then everyone began drifting back toward the cars, and Eve did not follow them.

She knelt and set the daisies against the headstone. That morning, before anyone knocked on her door, she had eaten two pieces of cinnamon toast and watched an old comedy special, and she had laughed out loud at one part, alone in the kitchen. Then she had stopped, mid-laugh, feeling like she had done something wrong. Nine days. It had only been nine days.

At school on Monday, she confided in Kash while they scraped leftover paint from the art room sink traps, a job Ms. Villanueva had assigned them for talking during the demo. "I laughed at a joke," Eve said, watching a blue flake spiral down the drain. "The week she died. Doesn't that make me a terrible person?" Kash was quiet for a second, which was unlike Kash. "My aunt printed out this thing when my grandpa passed. It's still on our fridge. A bunch of names on it."

After school they walked to Kash's house and stood in the kitchen reading the paper clipped to the fridge door under a magnet shaped like a pineapple. It was a page from a counseling office, and near the bottom it said that in 1999, researchers Margaret Stroebe and Henk Schut had described grieving people as moving back and forth between focusing on the loss and getting on with daily life. Kash tapped the line above it. "That's what it's called," Kash said. "The dual process model." Eve read the sentence twice. "So the laughing is the getting-on-with-daily-life part," she said slowly, "and it goes back and forth. It's not one straight line where you have to be sad the whole time or you failed." Kash shrugged. "My aunt says some days she only cooks his recipes and cries, and some days she just cooks."

The following Sunday, Eve's family drove back out to the cemetery with candles in paper cups, the small kind with the flammable lids you had to peel off carefully so the wax wouldn't spill. Her father lit one and set it by the daisies, which had gone brown at the edges. Eve stood with her hands in her jacket pockets and thought about the back-and-forth, how in one week she had cried in the shower on Tuesday and then on Thursday helped Alyvia film a video for the science fair, laughing at Alyvia's terrible volcano puns, and both of those days had been real days.

She peeled the lid off a second candle and cupped her hand around the flame while her mother dug a small groove in the soft dirt so it wouldn't tip. "She would have liked these," Eve said, nodding at the candles, and her mother said, "She kept them in the window at Halloween, every single year."

The wind chime two rows over rang once, and Eve watched the little flame bend and straighten, bend and straighten. Then she said, "I'm going to tell Kash about the cinnamon toast thing. The whole thing." She blew out the match and dropped it in the paper cup.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Psychologist Lee Ross named the fundamental attribution error in 1977: the tendency to blame others' actions on their personality while underestimating their situation.
story:
Ms. Toussaint wrote one word on the board, "interpretation," and then read a short paragraph about a boy who shoved past a girl in the hallway without saying a word. "What kind of person is he?" she asked.

"Rude," said Scarlet, without raising her hand all the way. "Total jerk move."

Muhammed, who sat near the window, said nothing. He was staring at his notebook, and Jasmine noticed that his pencil had stopped moving halfway through a sentence. She had a reason to pay attention to Muhammed today. Yesterday she had sworn he'd ignored her on purpose when she waved at him across the cafeteria, and she'd spent the evening being angry about it. Now she wanted to figure out whether she'd been right.

"Maybe he was late for something," Jasmine said. "The paragraph doesn't say what happened before the hallway." A few kids rolled their eyes, and one boy called her idea "controversial," which made no sense to her, since it wasn't like she'd taken a side in a war. Ms. Toussaint just said, "Keep going," so Jasmine decided to test it. She turned her notebook sideways and drew two columns. In one she wrote "jerk," and under it she listed everything that would have to be true for the shove to come from his personality. In the other she wrote "motive," and listed situations that could push even a polite person to shove: bad news, an emergency, a phone call he'd just gotten. The second column filled up faster.

That was when Muhammed finally spoke. "My grandfather went into the hospital this morning," he said quietly. "That's why I didn't wave back yesterday, Jasmine. I was reading the message." The room went still. Scarlet looked at her desk.

Ms. Toussaint pulled a book off the shelf and set it on the front table. "There's a name for what Jasmine just did," she said. "The fundamental attribution error." She passed the book around, and Jasmine read the page herself: the psychologist Lee Ross had named it in 1977. Blaming other people's actions on their personality while underestimating their situation. She copied the sentence into her notebook, then evaluated her two columns again. Every entry under "jerk" now looked flimsy, like a shelf nailed with one screw.

After the bell, Jasmine caught Muhammed at the door. "Is your grandfather going to be okay?"

"He's out of surgery," Muhammed said. "My mom says he's talking again." He pulled his backpack onto one shoulder. "You really made two whole lists about me?"

Jasmine held up the notebook, and Muhammed laughed, and together they walked out into the loud, crowded hall.

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: If clothes catch fire, the safety rule is stop, drop and roll, because running feeds the flames more oxygen.
story:
The permission slip had to be signed by third period, and Bentley had written his mom a note that morning: "Dear Mom, fire station trip on Friday. I want to be the one who gets picked for the demonstration. Please sign. Love, Bentley." She had signed it at the bus stop, her pen scratching against the brittle paper where the frost had stiffened it, and he had folded it into his pocket like a treasure map.

On Friday, Mr. Sinclair counted heads twice outside the red brick station, and the doors rolled up with a groan. The bay smelled of rubber hoses and motor oil, and somewhere a radio crackled. A firefighter in suspenders led them past the truck, past racks of boots standing like sleeping soldiers, to a wide gray mat on the floor.

"Who wants to help with a demonstration?" the firefighter asked, and every hand shot up, including Bentley's, stretched so high his shoulder ached. Lindsay raised hers halfway, and Brycen waved both of his like a man signaling a plane.

The firefighter's eyes swept the row. "You, with the green jacket. What's your name?"

"Bentley," he said, and his voice came out steadier than he expected.

"Ever heard of stop, drop and roll?" the firefighter asked.

"Yes. If your clothes catch fire, you stop, you drop, and you roll."

"That's it. Show us."

Bentley thought for a second before he moved. The night before, he had lain on his bedroom floor practicing, and something had clicked: running would only feed the flames oxygen, so the whole point was to stay still and smother them. He planted his feet, dropped flat onto the mat, and rolled, one shoulder over the other, the foam squeaking under his jacket.

"And why don't you run for help?" the firefighter asked the class.

"Because running feeds the flames more oxygen," Bentley said from the floor, and the firefighter gave him a thumbs up.

Lindsay went next, and she rolled too fast, tumbled off the mat, and popped up with red cheeks. "I violated the rule," she said. "I rolled like a log down a hill."

"You stopped, you dropped, you rolled," the firefighter said. "The order was right. Try it slower."

She did, and this time she stayed on the mat the whole way across. Brycen clapped so hard his hands must have stung, and Bentley stuck out his fist for her to bump. Before they left, he bought a postcard at the front desk, smelled faintly of smoke, and wrote on the back while the class lined up: "Dear Mom, I got picked. I didn't run. Bentley."

activity: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
knowledge_domain: to explain how the tilt of Earth's axis causes the seasons
fact: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees from straight up relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun.
story:
The globe in the corner of the planetarium lobby was leaning, and Daniel could not stop staring at it. Most globes stood straight on their stands, poles up and down, like good soldiers. This one tilted off to the side, and nobody else in the class seemed to think that was strange.

"Maybe somebody bumped it," Henrik said, giving the globe a hopeful nudge. It didn't straighten.

Trinity took a photo of the little plaque beside the stand and read it aloud. "It says Earth's axis is tilted about 23.4 degrees from straight up relative to the plane of its orbit around the Sun."

"So it's supposed to lean," Daniel said slowly. The real Earth, the actual planet they were standing on, was leaning right now, and had been leaning the whole time he'd been alive. He'd never once thought about it.

The trouble was the contest. In twenty minutes, each group had to stand in front of the museum's big Sun lamp and explain to a judge why we have seasons. Their whole presentation rested on one assumption, the one Daniel had written on the notecard in his own handwriting: seasons happen because Earth gets closer to the Sun at some times of year. He'd been proud of that sentence. Now the leaning globe was making it look shaky.

"Wait," he said. He borrowed a flashlight from the activity table and grabbed an orange from his lunch bag. He poked a pencil through the orange and held the pencil tilted, leaning it the way the globe leaned. "If distance caused seasons, the whole planet would be hot or cold at the same time. But when it's summer here, it's winter in Australia. My cousin lives there. She's told me." He moved the tilted orange in a slow circle around the flashlight, keeping the lean aimed the same way the whole trip around. One hemisphere caught the light more directly; the other got slanted rays. Then, halfway around, they switched.

"So it's the tilt," Trinity said, crossing out Daniel's notecard with what he felt was unnecessary enthusiasm.

"Can we cite the plaque?" Henrik asked, waving Trinity's photo.

When their turn came, Daniel held up the orange and the pencil and made the same slow circle under the big lamp. The judge, a volunteer in a vest covered in rocket pins, watched the hemispheres trade places. Ms. Ionescu, standing at the back, raised her eyebrows at the crossed-out notecard in Trinity's hand.

"First draft," Daniel said, and kept orbiting.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007, says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership.
story:
Carson had one job at the culture fair: guard the refreshment table. He did not mind. From his folding chair he could watch the whole gym, including the poster Avery had spent two weeks on, the one with maps and family photographs and the title "Métis on both sides of my family." Jannat stopped in front of it, arms crossed, studying it like she was skeptical of every word. Next to the poster hung Carson's own sloppy drawing of a sugar glider, left over from the science club's marsupial display, and he wished he were over there instead, hearing whatever Jannat was about to say.

He heard it anyway, because Jannat did not lower her voice. "You can't just decide you're Métis," she said. "You're not on any official list. My cousin married into a First Nation and they told her straight out that the community decides who belongs, not the person. So if the community decides, and your community hasn't decided, you're just... claiming something."

Avery's ears went red. Kids nearby had stopped pretending not to listen. One boy in a Raptors hoodie muttered, "Here we go," in a way that made Carson want to ridicule him, but the look on Jannat's face stopped him. She was not smirking. She was arguing like it mattered, like she was protecting somebody she loved.

"That's not how it works for First Nations, but Métis have their own ways," Avery said, and then Ms. Jean-Louis drifted past with a tray of cups and said only, "Why don't you look it up before you settle it?" and pointed at the library cart parked by the bleachers. There was a laptop on it. Jannat sat down first, typed fast, and read aloud in a flat, careful voice: "The United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, adopted on 13 September 2007, says Indigenous peoples have the right to determine their own identity and membership."

The gym went quiet enough that Carson heard the coffee urn gurgle. Jannat read the sentence again, slower, and Carson watched her work it through. Not the government. Not her cousin's story, either. The peoples themselves. "So nobody else gets to hand down the ruling," she said finally. "Not even me." She stood up and looked at the poster again, at the photographs of Avery's grandmothers. "I was arguing about a list. I wasn't arguing about you."

"I know," Avery said. "You were defending your cousin."

"That's not an excuse, but it's the reason." Jannat pulled out her phone. "I'm texting her. She's going to want to see that declaration."

Carson left the refreshment table, carried two cookies over, and set one beside each of them.

activity: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
knowledge_domain: to do a load of laundry from sorting colours to folding
fact: Dots on the iron symbol set the highest safe iron setting: one dot is low, about 110 degrees Celsius, two is medium, about 150, and three is high, about 200.
story:
Rosalie had agreed to take over the family laundry, every step of it, because her mother had agreed to sign the papers for a real bank account with her own name on it. The deal felt distinct from ordinary chores, more like a contract, so she sorted the clothes into darks and lights, ran the machine, and carried the warm basket upstairs to fold. Her last job was the shirt she planned to wear to the bank tomorrow, a slippery nylon thing with a collar that had dried into a wrinkle like a mountain range. She set the iron to cotton, pressed hard, and watched a shiny rectangle bloom across the front pocket, smooth and gleaming and completely wrong. She stood there feeling like the narrator of her own disaster documentary.

She flipped the shirt's tag over. Next to the tiny iron symbol sat a single dot. Her mother's cotton blouse, hanging nearby, had three dots beside its symbol. Rosalie hunted through the laundry basket until she found a tag with two dots, then lined all three tags up on the counter like evidence. She remembered the iron's dial, which had a low, a medium, and a high, and she remembered exactly where cotton had been. One dot had to mean low, around 110 degrees Celsius; two dots meant medium, about 150; three dots meant high, roughly 200. Her nylon shirt, with its single dot, had just met an iron hot enough for the three-dot crowd. She turned the dial to low, laid a pillowcase over the collar, and tested it on a corner. The wrinkle flattened. The shine did not spread. Good enough.

The next morning she wore the shirt into the bank with the shiny patch turned slightly toward her shoulder, hoping nobody would look. Charlie-Rose was already at the counter with a backpack full of rolled coins, saving up for a concert ticket and determined to deposit every last quarter before the price went up. Tatiana had come along to supervise and to eat the mints from the bowl by the deposit slips, one at a time, with great ceremony.

Ms. Tang called Rosalie up to the desk. "First account?"

"Yes. I'm paying in laundry money." Rosalie pushed the coins across, then, before she could stop herself, nodded at her shoulder. "Before you say anything, I know about the shiny part."

Ms. Tang tilted her head. "Iron?"

"Nylon, iron on the cotton setting," Rosalie said. "One dot means low, about 110 degrees. I used three dots on a one-dot shirt. It won't embarrass me twice." She said it lightly, though she had practiced the sentence on the walk over.

Charlie-Rose leaned in from the next window. "Wait, the dots mean something? I've been ironing everything on high since forever." She looked down at her own jacket sleeve, which had a faint sheen along the cuff, and pushed her coin rolls forward with new urgency.

Ms. Tang stamped the account form and slid it back. "Signature here. Then you're official."

Rosalie signed, took her temporary card, and turned to Charlie-Rose. "Show me your tag."

activity: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
knowledge_domain: to play a piece with dynamics and tempo changes in a band or on the piano
fact: The piano's full name is pianoforte, meaning soft-loud, because the player can make notes soft or loud by how hard the keys are struck.
story:
Max had quit piano lessons in October, and he'd regretted it ever since, especially now that the spring concert at the community centre was two weeks away. He stood in the small practice room, staring at the upright piano like it was a rival chess player. His friend Evelyn leaned against the wall, arms crossed.

"You quit for six months and now you want to play the solo," she said. "That's like skipping practice all season and demanding the ball at the final buzzer."

"I didn't demand anything. Ms. Kaminski asked." He set the music on the stand. "Besides, the notes aren't the problem. I can hit every note. It just sounds like a robot reading a grocery list."

"Then stop being a robot." She dropped into the folding chair beside him. "Play the loud part loud."

He played the loud part loud. The windows buzzed. Evelyn winced. "Okay, that's not loud, that's invasive. My ears would like a lawyer." He laughed and tried again, softer this time, and the passage flattened out into nothing, quiet in a way that felt like an apology.

Max stopped and looked at his own hands, which was when he remembered something his old teacher's colleague had said at a recital last spring, back before he quit. The man had tapped the sheet music and said, "It's not a piano, you know. It's a pianoforte. Soft-loud." Max had assumed that was just something old musicians said to sound impressive. Now he wondered if it was an instruction. The name itself was telling him the instrument could do both, that the whole idea of it was soft and loud, and that the difference lived in his fingers, not on the page.

He had to test it. He played the same phrase four times, changing only how hard he struck the keys, keeping his speed exactly the same. Soft, the melody crept. Harder, it strode. Harder still, it demanded attention. The notes were identical every time, but the feeling wasn't, and nothing on the page had changed at all. "It was in my hands the whole time," he said. "I was reading the letters and ignoring the volume."

He ran the piece straight through, letting the quiet verse tiptoe and the chorus surge, and when he finished, Evelyn was smiling.

"Better," she admitted. "Still not concert ready."

The door opened, and Ms. Kaminski poked her head in. "Max, small change to the programme. The other soloist caught the flu, so you'll be playing twice as long." She tapped the doorframe. "Can you learn the second piece by Friday?"

Evelyn grinned. "He can't even play the first one softly."

"Oh, that part I figured out," Max said, and reached for the new music.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Muscles in a limb kept still in a cast weaken and shrink, which is why an arm often looks thinner when the cast comes off.
story:
Kaylee pressed her thumb into the fresh skin of her left arm and watched the dent stay there like clay. Six weeks of cast, and now the arm looked like it belonged to somebody younger, somebody in third grade. Next to her on the clinic bench, her right arm lay plump and ordinary, and the difference was so strange she held both wrists together to check she was not imagining it.

"I look like I got two different people's arms," she said to Jamie, who had come along after school so they could walk to the playground together.

"That's so weird," Jamie said. "It was the same size before, right?"

Kaylee turned it over in her mind all the way to the schoolyard fence. The bone had healed; the doctor had said so. But the arm had been wrapped up and still for six weeks, and muscles kept still in a cast weaken and shrink, and that had to be why it looked thinner. She hadn't used it, so it had gone small. It made a kind of cold, clean sense, like a math proof.

At the monkey bars, Lilliana was already hanging upside down by her knees, calling out challenges. "Kaylee! You said first day without the cast, you'd demolish my record. Seven bars, no stopping."

"I said it before I saw this thing." Kaylee held up the thin arm. But she wanted that record more than she wanted to admit, so she stood under the first bar and made a plan. Her right arm was strong enough to carry most of the work. She would grip with the right, and let the left just hold on, like a clip, testing whether it could even do that.

She jumped, caught the first bar with her right hand, swung, and slapped the left palm onto the second bar. The grip held, barely. She swung again. On the third bar, the left arm shook like a wet noodle, and on the fourth her fingers slid off and she dropped into the wood chips.

Lilliana hung there, blinking. "That was four. Not seven."

Kaylee sat in the chips, flexing her small left hand open and closed. "It's weaker than I thought. It faded while I was in the cast. So the record has to wait until the muscle comes back."

"Ms. Hamdan will make you a training chart," Jamie said. "You know she will. She's got that whole eccentric system of labeling everything with sticky notes, heritage recipes taped inside her cupboard door, half a wall of charts."

"Good," Kaylee said. "Tell her to label this one skinny left arm, coming back." She stood up, brushed off the chips, and walked back to the first bar.

activity: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
knowledge_domain: to describe their family and pets in a new language using full sentences
fact: French possessive words agree with the thing owned, not the owner, so "sa mère" can mean either "his mother" or "her mother."
story:
Ms. Bianchi handed out the speaking assignment like she was dealing cards: describe your family and your pets, in French, in full sentences, by Friday. Jayden had a mother, a stepfather, a little sister, and a cat named Bishop who only loved people who ignored him. That was plenty of material. The problem was the sentences, which kept coming out wrong in ways nobody would explain.

He practiced in the cafeteria with Jayla, who took French too. "Mon chat s'appelle Bishop," he said. "Il est noir. Et... sa mère est grise." Jayla frowned at her tray. "Bishop's mother is grey?" "No, no. MY mother. My mom." He looked at his notes. "I wrote sa mère. Why did I write that?" "Maybe because you copied it off Ruben's poster," Jayla said, and went back to her sandwich, which was the most useful thing anyone said all week.

He found Ruben after last period. Ruben's poster was on the wall by the gym, decorated with a defiant orange border, as if the poster itself were ready to argue. In careful letters it said Ma mère s'appelle Denise. Sa mère s'appelle Marie. Jayden stared at it. Marie was Ruben's grandmother, he was almost sure. So sa mère meant grandmother now? He said the two lines out loud, twice, and something shifted. Sa mère, sa mère. The word sa hadn't changed. Maybe sa didn't care whose it was at all. Maybe it only looked at the thing owned. He tested it against Jayla's sentence about her dog, which he remembered was sa chienne, and Ruben's, also sa chienne, and his own note about his grandmother, sa grand-mère, which he had definitely copied from somewhere.

"Ruben," he said. "On your poster. Sa mère est Marie. Is Marie your grandma?" Ruben squinted. "Yeah. My mom's mom." "So sa mère there means his mother? Like, Denise's mother?" "I guess," Ruben said, in the voice of someone discovering he'd built a bridge without knowing how.

In class on Friday, Jayden read his sentences. "J'ai un chat. Mon chat s'appelle Bishop. Ma sœur adore le chat, mais le chat adore ma mère." Then he paused. "Et voici le piège," he said, and waited. Ms. Bianchi raised an eyebrow. Jayden held up his card, where he'd written one sentence: Sa mère a un chien. "Ruben," he said. "Whose mother has a dog?" Ruben read it. "Mine?" Jayden turned to Jayla. "Or yours?" Jayla read it. "Could be mine." Nobody in the room could tell from the sentence alone. That was the trick, and Jayden had found it by accident and then on purpose, which was his preferred order.

He got his marks back Monday. The one criterion he'd missed was "clear sentences," circled twice. Jayla leaned over. "So sa mère can mean his mother OR her mother? That's it?" "That's it," Jayden said. "The listener has to ask." He picked up his pencil, crossed out half his draft, and started writing questions.

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: In Python, the % operator gives the remainder of a division, so n % d == 0 is true exactly when d divides n evenly.
story:
Julia had promised her classmates a working program by Monday, and so far all her program did was crash. She sat at the kitchen table with her mom's old laptop open, a notebook beside her, and a message from Daniyal glowing on her screen: "Emaan says your prime checker told her 9 is prime. Fix it before class, please." She pressed Enter again, typed 9, and there it was, "prime," confident and completely wrong.

The problem wasn't the whole idea. She had learned in Mr. Tanaka's club that a prime number has no divisors except 1 and itself, and she had written a loop that tried every number up to n and checked something. The something was where it fell apart. She had written "if n / d" and then guessed at what to do next, and obviously the guessing had gone badly.

She stared at the line until the words seemed to slide around. Then she grabbed a pencil and worked it out on paper like Mr. Tanaka kept telling them to. If she divided 9 by 3, she got 3 with nothing left over. If she divided 9 by 4, she got 2 with 1 left over. The pattern was about what was left over, not the answer. "It's like a trial," she muttered. "The number is the defendant, and every smaller number gets to testify whether it divides evenly." Her mom looked over from the sink, and Julia waved her off, already halfway to the manual.

The table of operators was short, and she found it near the bottom of the arithmetic page. The percent sign. She read the line twice, then flipped back a page to make sure she wasn't confusing it with percentages. She typed a quick test in the shell: 9 % 3. The screen printed 0. Then 9 % 4 printed 1. So the percent sign gave back the remainder of a division, nothing more and nothing less, which meant that if n % d came out as 0, d had divided n evenly, with nothing left over. That was the whole trick. It had been sitting there the entire time.

She deleted her broken line and wrote the new one: if n % d == 0, mark the number as not prime and stop. Then she thought about the edge cases, because 9 had humiliated her once already. The number 2 was prime even though it was trivial to forget, and 1 wasn't prime at all, and her loop should probably not waste time dividing by 1. She scratched out notes, crossed two of them out, and clarified her plan in the margin in small letters: check 2 first, then only odd numbers up to the square root, since anything bigger would have to pair with something smaller.

The kitchen went quiet except for her keys. She ran the program and typed 9. "Not prime." She typed 97. "Prime." She typed 25, 2, 1, 100, 7, and the answers came back correct every time, so fast that the screen seemed to answer before she finished pressing Enter. She copied the file onto her flash drive, then pasted the whole thing into a message to Daniyal with one line on top: "Emaan can test it herself, but tell her 9 says not prime now."

A reply buzzed back within a minute. "She says the defendant is guilty. See you Monday."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: In the United States, the USDA says a 'best if used by' date shows when a food will be at its best quality; it is not a food-safety date.
story:
Paisley had promised herself she would not embarrass herself on her first morning at the food bank, and she was already breaking that promise. She stood in the sorting room holding a clipboard, and every category on it seemed designed to confuse her. Canned vegetables went in the green bins, pasta in the blue, and anything damaged went to a shelf marked HOLD. Behind her, Ivan was stacking jars of peanut butter like a tower, and Alexi was sliding cans down the table in a game she had invented where nothing ever actually fell.

"Careful," Paisley said, but the coach in charge had already assigned her to the date-checking table, and a small line of donated groceries waited there. Her job was simple, according to the vague instructions taped to the table: sort out anything too old. She had checked maybe fifteen boxes when she came to a cereal box stamped with a date that was yesterday's.

"Rejected," said a woman beside her, reaching to toss it into the bin. Paisley almost let her. Then she thought about her own kitchen, where her mother's crackers lived in the pantry weeks past their stamped date and nobody had ever gotten sick. The stamp didn't say "unsafe after." It said something else, she was almost sure, something her mother had once read aloud off a label: "best if used by." That wasn't a warning. That was the company saying the food would taste its best before then, not that it turned dangerous the day after.

"Wait," Paisley said. "I don't think that's a safety date. I think it just shows when it's at its best quality. Like day-old bread." The woman paused, cereal hovering over the bin, and squinted at the stamp. "Hmm. That would explain all the pasta we throw out." Paisley tested her idea the only way she could: she turned the box over, found a phone number, and called it while the woman watched. The person on the line confirmed it, in the plainest words. The woman exhaled and put the cereal into the shelf-ready crate instead of the trash.

Alexi spun around from her can game. "You just saved breakfast for somebody." Ivan abandoned his peanut butter tower to look at the pile behind the date table, and his face changed, because Ivan had a secret: he had been quietly horrified all morning by how much food was going into the trash. "Can we go back through the bin?" he asked the coach. "Just the stuff that's one or two days past?"

The twist came when the coach, who had run this room for six years, admitted she had never been sure about those stamps either and had always played it safe. "I thought I was protecting people," she said, and Paisley understood that the real risk had been the opposite, throwing away boxes of perfectly good cereal while families waited outside. She was glad she had spoken up instead of standing there in silent humiliation, assuming the grown-ups knew everything.

By lunchtime, the four of them had rescued a whole crate from the trash bin, and Alexi had written BEST IF USED BY on a sticky note and posted it above the table, with an arrow pointing at the calendar. A man carrying a toddler came through the line just before noon and chose the recovered cereal, holding it up so the little girl could see the toucan on the box. She grabbed for it with both hands, and Ivan whispered, "That's my tower's best customer."

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In March 1933, Joseph Goebbels became head of Nazi Germany's new Reich Ministry of Public Enlightenment and Propaganda.
story:
Audrey flopped onto the couch between Rory and Kingsley, holding the museum flyer they'd gotten from Mr. Tran's class trip. The exhibit on World War II had ended with a wall of glossy posters, all bright colors and bold slogans, and her head was still buzzing from them. "Did you see the one with the athlete?" she said. "And the movie star one? Why would a movie star be on a government poster?"

"Because everyone likes movie stars," Kingsley said, reaching over her to steal a handful of popcorn from the bowl on the coffee table. Rory elbowed him gently and slid the bowl closer to Audrey first, because she always got stuck in the middle and never got any.

Audrey took a handful and frowned at the flyer. Something about those posters had itched at her the whole bus ride home. They hadn't just shown facts. One poster said the whole nation was behind a plan, as if disagreeing meant you were alone. Another used words like "rot" and "decay" for the other side, words that made her stomach twist before she'd even thought about what they meant. "They weren't trying to tell us things," she said slowly. "They were trying to make us feel things."

Mr. Tran had said one sentence at the poster wall before letting them wander, something about a propaganda ministry created in March 1933, with Joseph Goebbels appointed to head it. Audrey had scribbled it in her notebook because it seemed important, and now she dug the notebook out of her backpack and read it aloud. "A whole government department just for this," she said. "Somebody planned those posters. The movie star, the 'everyone agrees' part, the nasty words. Those were choices."

Rory sat forward. "So it's like the ads for those sneakers Kingsley bought."

"Hey," Kingsley said, but he was grinning. "The ad had a famous basketball player in it."

"Exactly." Audrey grabbed the remote and pulled up a sneaker ad on the TV. They watched a stadium full of cheering fans, a slogan about everyone switching brands, and a voice-over calling other shoes "flimsy junk." Audrey pointed at each one. "Celebrity. Bandwagon. Loaded words. Same tricks, different poster." She paused. "I think being able to spot the tricks is a factor in not getting fooled. Like a checklist you run in your head."

"It's not feasible to check every single ad, though," Rory said. "There are millions."

"Then we practice," Audrey said. She clicked to the next ad, a cereal commercial with a pop singer and a line about what "smart families" eat. "Go. First one to name all three tricks picks the movie tonight."

Kingsley leaned in, eyes narrowed at the screen. "Singer... everyone's doing it... and 'smart families,' that's the loaded one." He pumped his fist. "I pick."

Audrey laughed and tossed him the last of the popcorn, right into his open hands.

activity: playing on a sports team for the season
knowledge_domain: playing on a sports team for the season
fact: In 1913 Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller.
story:
The hockey team had lost four games in a row, and the coach had run out of patience with drills, so on Friday she marched them off the ice and into the corridor behind the rink where the Zamboni slept. She looped a thick rope around a steel post and split the team in half. "Tug-of-war," she said. "Until you learn to pull together." Raphael wiped the sweat off his forehead and grabbed the rope beside Miko, who had been sulking ever since the coach picked Matilda as assistant captain instead of him.

They won the first pull easily because Matilda's side had only four players against their six. The second time, the coach added two more boys to Matilda's side, and then a third, until eight of them were hauling against six. Raphael's arms burned and his skates, still on his feet, slid on the concrete. They lost. But that wasn't the strange part. The strange part was that eight people hadn't pulled anything like eight times harder than one. It felt barely stronger than six.

That night Raphael sat at the kitchen table with cocoa cooling beside him and typed "why do big groups pull weakly on ropes" into the library computer. What came up made him sit straighter. In 1913, a man named Max Ringelmann reported that as more people pulled on a rope together, each person's average pull became smaller. He read it twice, then three times. So it wasn't just his team being lazy. It was a real thing, something you couldn't see on the rope itself but could infer from how weakly the whole group moved. He wondered whether you could fight it, the way you fight friction on ice by sharpening your blades.

At Monday practice, the coach set up the rope again, and Raphael raised his hand. "Can we try something? Put eight on each side, but make everybody shout a count, like one, two, pull, together."

The coach raised an eyebrow. "You think shouting makes ropes stronger?"

"I think it makes each person remember they're pulling." He didn't say the name Ringelmann out loud. He just wanted the test.

They tried it. "One, two, PULL!" echoed off the cold glass doors of the rink, and the rope jumped like something frightened. Miko, counting loudest of anyone, leaned back so far he nearly sat down, and his side dragged Raphael's side four full metres across the floor.

Afterward Miko handed Raphael his water bottle, which he had never done before. "Okay," Miko said, still breathing hard. "I thought the counting stuff was ridiculous. It wasn't." He looked over at the rope, coiled now beside the Zamboni like a sleeping snake. "Same time next practice?"

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: Judgment words such as best, worst, beautiful, boring and should are often signs that a sentence expresses an opinion.
story:
Kayla flopped onto Axel's kitchen table and pushed her laptop toward him. "Mr. Costa says half our homework grade is this," she said. "We have to find five opinions in product reviews and say why each one is an opinion. It's so tedious I almost fell asleep on the keyboard."

Axel pulled a bag of chips from the pantry and slid into the chair beside her. On the screen were reviews of a blender. One read, "This is the best blender on the market, and the jars are beautiful." Another said, "The motor runs at 12,000 revolutions per minute and weighs four pounds."

"Okay," Kayla said, talking mostly to herself. "Best. Beautiful. Those have to be opinions, right? But why? That's the part Mr. Costa wants." She highlighted the word best and stared at it until her eyes stung from the screen.

"Try this one," Axel said, tapping a third review. "'This blender should be cheaper for what you get.' Is should an opinion?"

Kayla read it twice. Something was ticking in the back of her mind, the way it did when she couldn't find her shoes and kept running through where she'd been. She scrolled back up and looked at the words she had marked: best, beautiful, should. Then she looked at the words she hadn't marked: runs, weighs, 12,000. The unmarked words could all be checked. Anyone could weigh the blender. Anyone could look it up.

"Wait," she said, sitting up so fast the chair squeaked. "The checkable ones don't have those judgment words in them. It's the other words. Judgment words such as best, worst, beautiful, boring and should are often signs that a sentence expresses an opinion." She said it slowly, testing it. "That's the pattern. That's what I highlight."

"Test it on this one," Axel said, grinning. He typed "worst blender ever boring to use" into the search box, and a review with exactly those words invaded the results page. Kayla highlighted worst and boring, then wrote beside them, "No way to check these. Opinion."

They worked through two more reviews, racing each other, and by the time the porch light outside had gone from gold to gray, Kayla had a page full of colored words. Mr. Costa walked in from next door to return Axel's dad's drill, glanced at the screen, and raised his eyebrows. "Nice work. You found the trick."

"I found it myself," Kayla said, and hit save.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: The Internet Archive's Wayback Machine has saved more than one trillion web pages, so something deleted from a public website can sometimes still be found.
story:
Keira had written a poem about mold for the class science blog, and by third period she regretted every line of it. The poem described mushrooms as "nature's silent decomposers" and rhymed that with "posey," which Ivan had read aloud in the cafeteria until Bryn laughed so hard she knocked over her milk. Worse, the post included a drawing meant to depict Keira dressed as a fungus, wearing a defiant little cap of construction paper. The whole school blog was public. Anyone could see it. She asked Ms. Charles after class if she could take it down, and Ms. Charles said it was her post, so of course she could.

At lunch Keira found the computer lab open and quietly empty, the machines humming in their rows. She logged in, found her post, and deleted it. Then she deleted Ivan's comment too, the one that said "THE POSEY LINE." She sat back, relieved, and watched the screen refresh to a blank spot where the poem had been. Bryn slid into the seat beside her a minute later, backpack still on.

"You erased the whole thing?" Bryn asked.

"Every word. It's gone."

Bryn tilted her head. "My cousin says nothing on the internet is really gone. She says the Internet Archive has this thing called the Wayback Machine, and it has saved more than one trillion web pages."

Keira frowned at the blank screen. "A trillion pages of what?"

"Of anything. Public websites. It saves copies." Bryn shrugged. "She said it when our aunt deleted her bakery site and then wanted an old photo back."

Keira did not believe it, exactly, but she could not stop wondering. A deleted page was like a hole in the ground, and she wanted to know if something was still buried in it. She typed the blog's address into the search box on the Wayback Machine site and waited while a grid of dates appeared, each one linked to a saved copy. One date was from the night her poem had gone up. She clicked it.

The blog bloomed back onto the screen, banner and all, exactly as it had been. She scrolled down past Ivan's post about mealworms and there it was: her poem, her drawing, the defiant little mushroom cap, even "THE POSEY LINE." It had not been online for two hours, and yet here it sat, patient and complete, like a photo pinned in a yearbook. She and Bryn looked at each other across the humming lab.

"So deleting it didn't matter," Bryn said slowly.

"It mattered for the blog," Keira said. "Just not for this." She read the first line of her poem again and, instead of cringing, felt something settle. The picture showed a mushroom standing in a forest, doing its quiet job, and honestly it was a decent drawing. She turned to Bryn. "Okay, new plan. I'm rewriting it. Better rhymes, no posey."

Bryn grinned and pulled her chair closer. "First line has to keep decomposers."

"Deal," said Keira, and she opened a blank page.

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In Spanish, a la izquierda means to the left, so la primera calle a la izquierda means the first street on the left.
story:
Aria sat in the back row of Mr. Goldberg's Spanish class, tracing the words "a la izquierda" over and over on the margin of her notebook until the ink went thin. The class project was tomorrow: each student had to call a real bakery in Seville, in Spanish, ask for directions, and understand the answer well enough to repeat it back. Aria's partner, Valentina, wanted the good grade desperately, because her older sister had inherited all the family trophies and Valentina intended to start her own collection.

"Ask me again," Valentina said, pulling her chair around. "I'll be the baker."

"Perdón, ¿dónde está la panadería?" Aria asked.

"Siga derecho y tome la primera calle a la izquierda," Valentina recited from the textbook, chewing her pen.

Aria froze. "Wait. Which street? The second one?"

"The first. La primera calle a la izquierda." Valentina tapped the page. "You keep mixing them up, and tomorrow if you walk the wrong way on the phone call, Mr. Goldberg counts it wrong."

Aria stared at the phrase. She said it slowly, breaking it apart like a dropped cookie. A la izquierda meant to the left, she was sure of that part. So if the whole thing meant the first street on the left, then the street she wanted was the very first one, not the second, not the one after the plaza. She tested it on Lyra, who sat diagonally ahead and turned around whenever Spanish got interesting.

"Lyra, if someone tells you la primera calle a la izquierda, how many streets do you pass before you turn?"

"Zero," Lyra said. "You turn at the first one on the left. Even I know that, and I spent most of Tuesday drawing on my wrist."

Aria wrote it down in block letters and covered the page with her hand before Valentina could see how reckless her handwriting had become, all jagged loops and crossed-out words. Then she made Valentina run the dialogue three more times, and each time she repeated the directions back, waiting until Valentina nodded before moving on.

The next day Mr. Goldberg set the speaker phone on his desk and dialed the bakery himself, arms crossed. When the baker answered, the classroom smelled like the chalk dust and someone's strawberry lip balm, and Aria's mouth went dry.

"Perdón, ¿dónde está la panadería?" she managed.

The baker's voice crackled. "Siga derecho y tome la primera calle a la izquierda."

"So, la primera calle a la izquierda," Aria repeated. "The first street on the left."

There was a pause, then the baker laughed warmly and said, "¡Sí, exactamente!"

Valentina pumped both fists. Mr. Goldberg wrote something in his grade book, and Aria, still holding her breath, finally let it out.

activity: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
knowledge_domain: to chop an onion safely with the claw grip and make a pasta sauce from scratch
fact: If a knife starts to fall, step back and let it drop; trying to catch a falling knife is a common way to get cut.
story:
The onion sat on Grandma's cutting board like a dare, papery skin crackling under Mya's fingers. River was coming over at five to film her first real cooking video, "Sauce From Scratch," and the sauce had to simmer for at least an hour, which meant the chopping had to happen now. Mya curled her fingertips under, the way Grandma had shown her that morning, knuckles forward like a claw, and set the blade against the onion.

"You're going to be famous," River had texted, followed by eleven fire emojis. Mya had read it four times.

The claw grip felt awkward, like writing with her left hand, but she persisted, and the first slice fell away clean. Her eyes began to sting and stream, and she laughed through the burn, blinking at the ceiling. Somewhere behind her the old fridge hummed and clicked, and the mixer on its shelf gave a small jolt of voltage as the compressor kicked on, rattling the counter.

The rattling was what did it. The knife, balanced too near the edge, slid sideways off the board and dropped toward the floor. Mya's hand shot out on pure instinct before her brain caught up, and she yanked it back and jumped away so fast she knocked the pepper mill off the shelf. The knife hit the linoleum with a clang and lay there, blade flat, harmlessly gleaming. River, who had just walked in with the camera raised, froze in the doorway.

"You just moved away from it," River said, lowering the camera. "I was about to grab it."

"Don't. Ever," Mya said, her heart still thudding. "If a knife starts to fall, you step back and let it drop. Trying to catch a falling knife is a common way to get cut. Grandma told me this morning, and I didn't really get it until my hand was already halfway there." She picked the knife up by the handle, washed it, dried it, and set it dead center on the board, where it belonged. "It's kind of ironic. The whole time I was worried about chopping my fingers with the claw grip, and the dangerous part was the counter."

"Can I film that part?" River asked, already rewinding. "The knife drop? People need to see it."

"You'll get a reenactment with a wooden spoon, and you'll like it." Mya squared her shoulders over the onion. "Now watch this claw grip. We have a sauce to build and my parents walk in at six-thirty."

"Rolling," River said, and the little red light came on.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: At 5 percent interest compounded once a year, $1,000 grows to $1,276.28 after five years.
story:
Jeremy counted the quarters twice before pouring them into the jar. The lemonade stand had earned forty-one dollars in two hours, mostly because Mr. Carvalho had ridden past on his cargo bike with three crates of lemons and told half the street about it.

"That's for the savings plan," Carolina said, pointing at the jar. "Remember, your grandfather's deal."

Jeremy's grandfather had offered it at dinner on Sunday: bring him one thousand dollars to hold, and he would pay Jeremy fifty dollars every year for five years. "Five percent," he had said. "Same as the bank, but I keep it in my safe and you get to see it."

Carolina stacked cups while he did the math on the back of a napkin. Fifty dollars a year, five years, that was two hundred fifty in interest, so twelve hundred fifty dollars at the end. It sounded solid.

Then Elyane rode up and dropped her bike in the grass. She had a folded flyer from the bank on Main Street. "My mom made me read this," she said. "Five percent, compounded once a year. I did it on my calculator during study hall." She turned the flyer over, where she had written the numbers in green pen: 1,000 at 5 percent compounded yearly grows to 1,276.28 after five years.

Jeremy took the pen and circled the last line. Twelve seventy-six against twelve fifty. Twenty-six dollars and twenty-eight cents more, from the same five percent. He read the word again. "Compounded," he said slowly. "That's what makes the difference."

"It's the interest earning interest," Elyane said, shrugging. "Don't ask me how. The calculator just kept giving me bigger numbers each year."

Elyane had her own plan for the lemonade money, which was concert tickets in October. She pulled the flyer toward her across the table and looked at it for a while. "Actually," she said, "my fifty dollars would turn into sixty-three and change by then. Not tickets. The account." She got her phone out and started typing a note to her mother.

Jeremy folded the napkin into his pocket. On Monday he would petition his grandfather for the same deal the bank offered, and if he said no, Jeremy knew exactly which door on Main Street he would walk through, flyer in hand.

Mr. Carvalho pedaled past again, waved, and called out, "Save me a cup for the ride home!"

"Coming right up," Jeremy said, and reached for the pitcher.

activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: Babies under one year should be put to sleep on their backs, on a firm, flat surface with no pillows, blankets or toys, which lowers the risk of sudden infant death.
story:
Carter's cousin had the perfect setup: a big house, a playpen in the corner, and neighbors on both sides who actually needed a sitter. That was how Carter ended up at his cousin's place on a Friday night, watching eight-month-old Mia while her parents were at a dinner two streets over. His friend Jonas had come along, mostly because Jonas wanted to practice his magic tricks on someone who couldn't walk away.

"I need a real audience," Jonas said, fanning out a deck of cards. "Babies are honest. If she laughs, I'm good."

"Feed her first," Carter said, checking the note the parents had left on the counter. It was longer than he expected. There was a section about bottles, a section about the emergency numbers, and a section with the heading SAFE SLEEP in capital letters.

Mia drank her bottle, drooled on Jonas's best card, and then rubbed her eyes with both fists in a way that Carter was starting to recognize as the signal. He carried her into the little room where the crib was set up. The parents had left a stack of folded things beside it, and Jonas had already grabbed the top one, a fluffy yellow blanket with a bunny on it.

"Here," Jonas said. "Babies love stuff like this, right? She can cuddle with the bunny."

Carter held up the note. "It says babies under one year go to sleep on their backs, on a firm, flat surface, with no pillows, no blankets, and no toys in the crib."

Jonas stared at the fluffy blanket like it had betrayed him. "So the bunny's out?"

"The bunny's out. The blanket too. Everything's out." Carter looked into the crib. It was already bare, just a tight fitted sheet on a firm mattress, and now he understood why. He laid Mia down on her back, and she blinked up at the ceiling, unbothered by the missing bunny.

"That seems kind of mean," Jonas said.

"It's what the note says." Carter was not going to argue with a note written by two parents who had clearly thought about this a lot. He had almost made an impulsive grab for the blanket himself a second before reading it, and the thought of what he might have done made his stomach tighten.

Mia fussed for a minute, and Carter patted her chest gently the way the note suggested, careful to keep his hand from becoming a pillow. He tried to categorize her sounds to figure out what she wanted: the whiny hiccups meant tired, the full-on wail meant something hurt, and this medium fussing seemed to mean she just wanted company. He kept patting until the fussing shrank to a murmur, then to slow breathing.

"So my whole act is ruined," Jonas whispered from the doorway. "She fell asleep before the finale."

"You can do it for me," Carter whispered back. "I'll be a tough crowd."

Jonas grinned and spread the cards on the kitchen table, keeping his voice low. He performed a trick where a chosen card jumped to the top of the deck three times in a row, and Carter honestly could not see how he did it. "Okay, that's genuinely good," Carter admitted. "How many times did you practice that?"

"Like two hundred. That's a ratio of two hundred practices to one impressed audience member, and it was worth it."

They sat in the quiet kitchen with the monitor between them, listening to Mia breathe. Every so often Jonas glanced at the baby screen like he was checking on his audience. When the parents came back and Carter told them exactly how bedtime had gone, back, firm mattress, nothing in the crib, the mother squeezed his shoulder and said they'd ask for him again. Jonas picked up his deck of cards and held it out toward the crib. "Next time," he whispered, "she stays awake for the finale."

activity: learning to play a musical instrument
knowledge_domain: learning to play a musical instrument
fact: The treble clef is also called the G clef because its curl circles the staff line for the note G.
story:
Emmett pressed his trumpet to his lips for the fourth time and missed the same note again. The sound came out flat and sad, like a goose with a cold. Across the band room, Ilya was already playing the whole first line of "Ode to Joy" without a single mistake, and Ms. Nwosu had twice told Emmett to watch his music instead of staring at the ceiling.

"Whatever," Darien whispered from the next chair. "It's just one note. It's basically trivial."

"It's not trivial," Emmett whispered back. "It's G. The line starts on G, and I keep hitting F instead."

After class, Ms. Nwosu kept him for two minutes. "Find the note before you play it," she said. "Use the map on the page." That was all she gave him, which felt like being handed a flashlight with no batteries.

At home, Emmett spread the sheet music on his bed and glared at it. Every single line began with the same squiggly symbol, the treble clef, curling and looping like a fancy signature. He had been ignoring it for weeks, treating it like decoration, the way some kids thought the flag on a mailbox was just for show. But Ms. Nwosu had said "map," and maps were not decoration. He grabbed a pencil and traced the swirl slowly, starting from the dot at the bottom, up through the tall stem, and around. The curl made a full circle, like a planet in a tiny orbit, and it looped around one particular line of the five on the staff. His pencil crossed that line twice, wrapping it.

Emmett sat up straight. He counted the lines from the bottom. One, two. The curl circled the second line up. He checked his fingering chart. The second line was G.

He hunted down his older sister in the kitchen. "Is the treble clef called the G clef?" he asked. "Because the curl circles the staff line for the note G."

She looked up from her sandwich. "That's literally what it's called. G clef. Some teachers even call it that."

The next morning in band, Emmett waited for the class to settle, his heart going fast. When they reached the first line, he didn't stare at the ceiling or guess. He traced the swirl with his eyes, followed its orbit down to the second line, and thought, that's G, that's home base. He lifted the trumpet and played the note, and it came out round and clear. He played the whole first line. It sounded like music.

Darien turned around in his chair. "Okay. Not trivial," he said.

Emmett tapped the clef on his stand with his pencil, once, like knocking on a friend's door. "Second line," he said.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: In his 1890 book 'Principles of Economics', economist Alfred Marshall compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors: it takes both to set a price.
story:
The last pint of strawberries at the market was marked eight dollars, and Emma winced at the sign. Last week the same berries had been four. "That's robbery," said Joyce, standing beside her at the table. "The seller just picks any number he wants."

"No way," said Ellen, shaking her head. "If he charged that much all summer, nobody would buy. Buyers decide the price, because we can walk away." They argued while a line formed behind them, six people deep, all of them eyeing the same single pint. Emma noticed that the next table over had a whole pyramid of zucchini, a mountain of it, and the sign there said fifty cents each. Two customers walked past it without even stopping. She turned the two pictures over in her mind, the crowded berry table and the lonely zucchini, and something clicked. Maybe both of her friends were right at the same time, which felt like a paradox she couldn't yet untangle.

She tested her idea by watching. When a woman ahead of her offered five dollars for the berries, the farmer shook his head, because three people behind her would pay eight. When a boy offered the zucchini farmer forty cents, he sighed and said fine, since the squash would only soften by Sunday. Emma counted on her fingers. Lots of buyers, few berries, high price. Few buyers, lots of squash, low price. It was the most probable explanation, and it meant the price wasn't chosen by just one side.

At Mr. Russo's stall, where he sold honey and used booklets about farming, Emma told him what she had seen. He nodded and pulled a thin old paperback from a crate. "Economist Alfred Marshall, in his 1890 book 'Principles of Economics', compared supply and demand to the two blades of a pair of scissors. It takes both to set a price." Emma imagined the two blades crossing over the number eight and understood: the farmer with the berries was one blade, and the long line of hungry customers was the other. Neither could cut alone.

She still wanted strawberries, though. Eight dollars was her entire allowance, money she had been saving for a new sketchbook. Then she saw Ellen eyeing the berries too, with only a crumpled two-dollar bill in her fist. Emma did some quick math out loud. "Split it with me? Four each." Ellen's face brightened, and Joyce dug through her pocket and produced a dollar. "I just want a handful," Joyce said, holding up the coins. "That's fair, isn't it? Three of us, three shares."

They carried the pint to a bench near the fountain and divided the berries into piles of small, medium, and large, taking turns choosing. Joyce got the biggest one, the lopsided giant at the bottom, and held it up like a trophy. Emma bit into her smallest berry, which was somehow the sweetest, and watched a new crate of strawberries arrive at the far table. The farmer chalked a new sign and turned it around: six dollars.

"See that," Ellen said, pointing. "Next week they'll be everywhere, and it'll be three dollars a pint."

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: In improv, 'yes, and' means accepting what your partner has established (yes) and then adding something new to it (and).
story:
On the second day of drama camp, Ms. Torres taped a sign to the mirror that said "YES, AND" and split everyone into pairs. Paige got Ethan, who was tall and funny at lunch but went silent the second a scene started. Their first exercise was a two-minute scene on a spaceship, and it died in forty seconds. Paige said, "Captain, the engines are failing." Ethan said, "Yeah." She waited, then said, "We need to land on that planet." Ethan said, "Okay." She stared at the carpet until Ms. Torres clapped the scene over.

At lunch Paige sat with Breanna, who was rehearsing a monologue under the bleachers because she wanted the lead in the Friday showcase more than she wanted dessert. "Ethan ruined our scene," Paige said. "He agreed with everything I said. You'd think agreeing would be good." Breanna kept her eyes on her script. "Maybe agreeing is the easy part," she said, and went back to her lines.

Paige chewed on that through afternoon games. When Breanna played a scene as a grumpy bus driver, Breanna accepted that Paige was a lost tourist, but she kept adding things: the bus was out of gas, the fare was a joke, the next stop was the moon. Every addition gave Paige somewhere to go. Paige thought back to Ethan. He had said yes with his mouth and no with his feet, because a yes with nothing after it was just a dead end. If the "yes" accepted what she had established, the "and" had to build something new on top of it, the way a foundation only mattered once you stacked walls on it.

Next morning she cornered Ethan by the prop table. "Do you actually want to do improv, or are you just being polite?" He exhaled, shoulders dropping. "I want to. I just never know what to say next. My brain goes blank and agreeing feels safe." Paige nodded. "Then don't try to be funny. When I say something, just add any one thing. Anything. Even if it's boring and conventional, like 'there's a door over there.'"

Their scene was in a haunted library. Paige said, "The bookshelf just moved." Ethan swallowed, then said, "Yeah, and the book it dropped is open to a page with our names on it." Paige's whole body woke up. "And the page says we owe the library a late fee." Ethan grabbed an imaginary coin from his pocket. "Then I'm paying with this chocolate coin I've been saving since second grade." Ms. Torres laughed out loud from the back of the room, and Paige grinned and lunged for the coin.

activity: building a project for the school science fair
knowledge_domain: building a project for the school science fair
fact: Two things happening together, called correlation, does not prove that one causes the other; another factor may cause both.
story:
Noah spread his graph across the library table and pressed the corners down with two dictionaries and a stapler. The line rose steadily: students who ate breakfast, on average, got better grades. He had surveyed ninety-two kids at school, and the pattern was so clean he could hardly sit still. His science fair project was going to prove that breakfast made kids smarter. That was the plan, anyway, until Zendaya dropped into the chair across from him and frowned at the graph.

"You surveyed who?" she asked, tapping the cluster of high points at the top of the line.

"Everyone in seventh grade who'd answer," Noah said. "Macie helped me hand out the forms at lunch."

"Then think about who actually filled them out. Kids who show up early enough to eat in the cafeteria. Kids like Macie, who does homework on the bus." She slid the graph toward herself. "My little brother eats pop tarts every single morning and he got a D in geography."

Noah pushed back from the table and rolled his pencil under his palm. Something about her objection itched at him. He stared at the rising line and tried to imagine breakfast actually causing it, the way gravity causes a dropped ball to fall. But two things could rise together without one driving the other. Maybe something else, some third thing, pushed both up at once. Kids who got enough sleep, maybe, or kids whose parents were around in the morning. If that hidden thing governed breakfast and grades together, then breakfast itself might be doing nothing at all. He had read a word for this in one of Ms. Russo's science books, and now he went back to the shelf and pulled it down, running his finger down the index until he found the page. Correlation. He whispered it aloud. Two things happening together was called correlation, and correlation did not prove that one caused the other.

He wrote it at the top of a fresh notecard, then flipped the card over and wrote his new question: what was the hidden third thing? He needed more data, and he needed it before Saturday. On the back of a overdue-notice flyer he wrote a message and slid it to Zendaya: "Can you and Macie survey the same kids about bedtime? If kids who eat breakfast also sleep more, that changes everything. Meet me here tomorrow at four. Bring graph paper. Noah." Zendaya read it, folded it into her pocket, and said she'd be there, because she wanted her name on the winning project too.

The next afternoon the three of them filled in the new column, bedtimes in blue ink beside breakfast answers in black. The blue numbers lined up with the black ones almost perfectly. Kids who ate breakfast mostly slept earlier, and the few pop-tart kids who stayed up past eleven sat at the bottom of both lists. Noah taped the second graph next to the first, and the title he wrote across the top of the display board read: "Breakfast and Grades: Together, But Which One Is the Cause?" He stepped back and looked at it, his marker still uncapped in his hand.

"We're not saying breakfast doesn't matter," Macie said, reading over his shoulder.

"We're saying the graph can't tell us," Noah said. "Which is the honest answer." He capped the marker and squared the boards against the table's edge.

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles, known as the war guilt clause, made Germany accept responsibility for the loss and damage caused by the war.
story:
The war memorial stood at the edge of the park, a granite soldier staring over a bed of red flowers, and Lillian stood in front of it with her index cards sweating in her hand. Tomorrow she had to explain to the whole class how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War, and so far all she knew was that she didn't understand it. She had read the chapter twice. Punishments, payments, blame. The words slid off her like rain off the granite.

Behind her, Stevie sat on the memorial steps, arms crossed, jaw tight. Mariana paced. "They can't put this all on you," Mariana said. "Everyone was tossing that ball around. Everyone."

"Tell that to Mr. Demetriou," Stevie said. "He saw the ball hit the wreath, and he saw me nearest, so it's my detention and my letter home. Alone." His voice went flat. "I resent that more than anything that's happened at this school."

Lillian turned her cards over, thinking. At home she'd found the phrase in her textbook and copied it onto a card: Article 231 of the Treaty of Versailles, the war guilt clause, made Germany accept responsibility for the loss and damage caused by the war. Not shared responsibility. Not some of it. All of it, pinned on one country while the others walked away. She looked at Stevie, hunched and angry on the steps, and something clicked into place like a lock.

"Wait," she said slowly. "What if everyone had been throwing the ball, and only one person got blamed for the whole thing?" Stevie shrugged. "That's exactly what happened to me." "No, I mean bigger. After the First World War, lots of countries fought, but the treaty had a part called the war guilt clause. It made Germany accept responsibility for the loss and damage the whole war caused. Everything. Just them." She watched his face change, the anger turning into something more thoughtful. "So how would you feel, if you were Germany?"

"I'd be furious," Stevie said. "Not just at the punishment. At being named as the only guilty one when I knew it wasn't only me. I'd want to prove them wrong." He stopped. "Wait. That's what happened after? That's how it led to the next war?" Lillian nodded, and for the first time the chapter made sense to her too. Blame this heavy doesn't fade. It waits.

" empathy," Mariana said suddenly. "That's what you just did, Stevie. You felt what a whole country felt." She pulled two granola bars from her backpack and tossed one to Stevie. "Eat something nutritious. You look like the granite soldier."

Stevie took a bite, then stood up. "Come on. I'm going to find Mr. Demetriou and tell him the whole truth, all of it, my part included." He glanced at Mariana, who had gone very still, her half-unwrapped bar motionless in her hand. "Mariana? You coming?"

"Stevie," she said quietly, "there's something I have to tell you first."

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Setting an account to private limits who can see your posts, but anyone you have already accepted as a follower can still copy or share what they see.
story:
Annabelle had posted the photo to her private account only an hour before, and now it was on a stranger's page. She sat frozen at her computer in the school lab, staring at the image of the parliament of owls she had photographed at the wildlife centre on Saturday, seven of them lined along a branch, with her caption underneath and, in the corner, the blurry edge of her own shoe.

"Whoa," said Seth, leaning over from the next machine. "That's yours, right? That guy has, like, four hundred followers."

"It's private," Annabelle said. "My account. Only people I accepted can see it." She heard the words and then heard what they didn't cover, like a floor that stops halfway across a room.

Mr. Nielsen circled the lab, checking screens for the science assignment, and Annabelle minimized her browser until he passed. The assignment was on inherited traits, and Ashlyn two rows back was typing a paragraph about how eye colour was hereditary, but Annabelle couldn't digest a single fact about genetics right now. Someone had her photo. Someone she didn't know had it, and she could not see how it had travelled.

She opened her follower list. Forty-one names. She scrolled slowly, forcing herself to look at each one. Most were classmates, a cousin, a few friends from summer camp. Then a name she barely remembered: a boy named on the wildlife centre's volunteer sheet, someone she'd accepted months ago because he'd commented on a bird post and she'd clicked approve without really thinking. She had met him exactly once, at a table, for about four minutes.

Seth watched her scroll. "You think it was him?"

"I can test it," Annabelle said. She posted a new photo, a boring one of the lab keyboard, with a tiny blue dot drawn in the corner, visible only if you enlarged the image. Then she waited. Fifteen minutes. Twenty. When the stranger's page refreshed, there was the keyboard, blue dot and all, posted two minutes after hers.

"That's the whole path," Seth said quietly. "Your account's private, but private doesn't stop people you already let in."

"Right," Annabelle said. "Setting it private limits who can see my posts, but anyone I already accepted can still copy or share what they see." She had learned it the hard way, and it felt like a rule you could only learn by walking into it.

She removed the volunteer as a follower, deleted the owl photo, and posted a message to the rest of her list asking them to take down anything they'd shared. Then she saved the owls to a folder on the school drive instead, where only her class could reach it for the science project. The stranger's page showed the photo gone within the hour.

Mr. Nielsen stopped behind her chair. "Nice work on the owl photo for your project, Annabelle. The parliament shot. Where did you get it?"

"I took it," she said, and turned back to the screen, and started typing her own name in the search bar, just to check one more time.

activity: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
knowledge_domain: to compare simple and compound interest on a savings account over five years
fact: In the United States, the Truth in Savings Act of 1991 requires banks to state savings rates as an annual percentage yield, or APY, which includes the effect of compounding.
story:
On Saturday mornings Zachary swept the floor of Mr. Singh's electronics repair shop, and on Saturday mornings he also stared at the bank poster in the window next door. It advertised a savings account with an interest rate, and beside it a slightly higher number labeled APY. He leaned on the broom and squinted until the numbers almost made sense.

"Two rates," he said to Alayna when she stopped by with her bike. "Same account. Why would the bank print both, and why is one bigger?"

Alayna shrugged, and the shrug made him more determined, not less.
