At lunch he borrowed the shop's ancient calculator, which only cooperated if you pressed each key twice, and worked out five years of interest on two hundred dollars, first added once a year, then added every month and left to grow. The monthly pile grew faster, and not by a tiny amount. The gap between his two columns widened like a slow smile. That had to be it. The poster's bigger number already counted that gap.

He tested his idea the way Mr. Singh tested a circuit board, checking the voltage across a suspect part before pronouncing it dead. Keagan came in to drop off a broken game controller, and Zachary grabbed him. "You have a savings account. Look at the paper they gave you."

Keagan dug out a crumpled sheet from his backpack. There it was, the same pairing, rate and a slightly higher APY, and at the bottom a line about the Truth in Savings Act of 1991. "In the United States," Zachary read aloud, finger under the words, "banks have to state savings rates as an annual percentage yield, an APY, and it includes the effect of compounding." He read it twice because it felt like finding the secret rule of a game.

"So the bigger number is the real one," Keagan said.

"It's the honest one," Zachary said. His five-year columns suddenly meant something outside his notebook. He copied both totals onto a receipt, folded it, and pressed it into Keagan's hand. "Ask your dad to move your money. Look at the APY, not the other one."

Mr. Singh rang up a customer, then nodded at the bank window. "You've been staring at that poster for three weeks. Solve it?"

"Almost," Zachary said, which felt like an understatement the size of the poster itself. He picked up the broom, swept a dust pile toward the door, and paused with the handle in both hands.

"Monday," he told Alayna through the open doorway. "My mom's taking me to open an account. You're coming."

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: The King Holiday and Service Act, signed in 1994, made Martin Luther King Jr. Day a national day of volunteer service in the United States.
story:
Jeremy had signed the volunteer sheet mostly because Maxton would not stop poking his arm with a pencil until he did, and now it was a January morning with no school, and he was standing in a chilly warehouse behind the church on Delmore Street, wearing a hairnet. He had assumed the day off was just a day off. Lots of holidays were just days off, as far as he could tell.

The problem revealed itself fast. Ms. Katz, who ran the food bank, pointed at a wall of empty shelves and said the big delivery truck would arrive at noon, and the families would start lining up at one. Everything had to be sorted, counted, and shelved by then. Jeremy, Maxton, and Libby were the whole workforce, plus one man who mostly moved pallets and said nothing.

"I need thirty hours of service for confirmation by Friday," Maxton announced, stacking cans like a man who believed speed was a virtue. "Today is worth six. I did the math twice."

"Can you quantify the cans instead?" Ms. Katz called from the office. "I need numbers for the grant report."

While they worked, Jeremy kept snagging on a question he could not see the answer to. Why were they here at all? School was closed, which usually meant nobody volunteered anywhere. Then Libby, squinting at a poster near the freezer, read it out loud. "The King Holiday and Service Act, signed in 1994, made Martin Luther King Jr. Day a national day of volunteer service." She looked at her gloves. "So it's a day on, not a day off. Huh. That's why the whole town does this today."

Jeremy turned that over while he taped labels. It meant the empty shelves were not bad luck. Everyone had the same idea on the same Monday, donations spiked, trucks jammed, and somewhere a system got overwhelmed on purpose, sort of. He tested his idea on the numbers in front of him. The sign-in sheet by the door listed twenty-two volunteers so far, and it was not even ten o'clock. He counted the empty bins. Not enough, by his estimate, for a day this size.

He ran to the office. "Ms. Katz, we don't have enough bins for the truck. I counted."

She looked at the shelves through the lens of her glasses, which had slid down her nose, then looked at Jeremy. "The church basement has forty. Can you three get them before the driver calls?"

They got them, mostly because Maxton wanted a reason to sprint. The truck came at 11:52, the line started at 12:58, and the last can hit the shelf with ninety seconds to spare.

"Six hours," Maxton said, writing it down.

"You dropped a bin of soup," Libby said.

"Five and a half."

activity: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
knowledge_domain: to write a Python program that asks for a number and prints whether it is prime
fact: A prime checker must handle numbers below 2 separately, because 0, 1 and negative numbers are not prime, yet a divisor loop starting at 2 finds nothing to reject them.
story:
Maya typed RUN and the program printed its answer: 0 is prime. She stared at the screen in the school computer lab, then leaned over to Jai's monitor to compare.

"You didn't check 0?" Jai asked. His program said 0 was prime too.

"Mr. Menon said a prime has to have no divisors except itself and 1," Maya said. "Zero doesn't count. Watch." She entered 1, and the program said 1 is prime. She entered negative 5, and the program said negative 5 is prime.

Zane pulled his chair over. "Your loop starts at 2," he said, pointing at her code. "It tries divisors from 2 up, and when it finds none, it says prime."

Maya read the loop again. For 0, 1, and negative numbers, the loop found nothing to reject them, so they slipped through. She had assumed that a number with no divisors must be prime, but that was backwards. Those numbers weren't prime at all, and her loop simply never tested them.

"I have to handle them before the loop," she said. "Separately." She added a line above it: if the number is less than 2, print not prime, and skip the loop. She ran it on 0. Not prime. On 1. Not prime. On negative 7. Not prime. Then she tested 7, which was prime, and 8, which the loop caught with the divisor 2. She nudged Jai. "Put your number in mine."

Jai typed 11 and got prime. Zane confessed that his own program had the same problem and copied Maya's fix, though he claimed his motivation was saving time, not admitting she had found it first.

Maya saved her file and printed the code on the lab's frail old printer, which groaned and spat out the page half sideways. Mr. Menon walked past, picked it up, and read the line at the top of her loop.

"Who told you about that?" he asked.

"Nobody," Maya said. "The computer told me 0 was prime, and it was wrong."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: The Rubin vase, introduced by Danish psychologist Edgar Rubin in 1915, can be seen as either a vase or two faces, but not both at the same moment.
story:
Zahra's kitchen table was covered with glue sticks, and Gabriella still didn't have a poster for the science fair, which was in two days.

"It doesn't have to be huge," Zahra said, cutting black paper. "Mr. Qureshi just wants something about perception. You know, how the brain sees stuff."

Gabriella flipped through Zahra's art book for ideas. Then she stopped. One page showed a black-and-white picture, and she could have sworn it was a vase, a curvy white vase sitting on a black background. "This one's good," she said. "A vase."

Zahra leaned over and laughed so hard she knocked a glue stick onto the floor. "A vase? Gabi, those are two faces. Look, two profiles staring at each other. That's clearly what it is."

The argument that followed provoked a full investigation. Gabriella held the book close, then far away. She squinted. She crossed her eyes, which made Zahra laugh again. It was strange, because the longer she looked, the more she felt the picture flicker, like her brain couldn't decide. Sometimes she saw the vase, sometimes the faces, but never both at the same moment. She tested this. She tried to hold them together on purpose, staring until her eyes watered, and the two shapes just would not overlap.

"I've got an idea," she said, and grabbed a blank card. She copied the picture in thick marker, exactly, edge for edge. "You look at yours, I'll look at mine. Same drawing, different eyes."

They sat knee to knee at the table. "Faces," Zahra said instantly. "Vase," said Gabriella at the same second. Then Zahra gasped. "Wait. Now it flipped. Now it's a vase!"

It reminded Gabriella of last summer, when she and her cousin had argued about the color of the estuary near her aunt's house. Her cousin said brown, she said silver, and for a whole hour they'd photographed the same water at different angles, getting different answers from the same river. Same thing, different viewer. Maybe that was true for more than water.

"Okay, twist," Zahra said, holding up her phone. She'd found the picture online. "It's called a Rubin vase. Some psychologist made it, way back in 1915. Danish guy."

"Edgar Rubin," Gabriella read over her shoulder. "So the guy basically invented an argument."

"The best kind," Zahra said. "An argument where everyone's right."

Gabriella wrote her poster title in big letters: ONE PICTURE, TWO TRUE THINGS. Below it she pasted her copy of the image, and then, for her demonstration, she planned to make every visitor at the science fair say out loud what they saw first. She could already picture it: half of them saying vase, half saying faces, and every single one of them certain.

"Chronic arguers, both of us," Zahra said, capping the marker. "At least now we'll have proof we can't help it."

Gabriella tilted her head at the card one last time. "Vase," she said.

"Faces," said Zahra.

activity: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
knowledge_domain: to improvise a scene with a partner by accepting each offer with yes, and
fact: Blocking is rejecting or ignoring a partner's offer, such as saying 'we're not on a boat', and it usually stops the scene from moving forward.
story:
Rosalie stood in the wings of the school auditorium, holding a rubber chicken she had grabbed from the props bin for reasons she could no longer remember. Ms. Aydın had paired everyone up for improv, and Rosalie's partner was Elin, who was currently bowing to the empty seats as though they were full of influential critics.

"Remember," Ms. Aydın called from the third row, "accept every offer. Yes, and." She said it the way she said most things, as if it were a rule she intended to enforce with a whistle.

Their scene started fine. Rosalie held up the chicken. "Grandma, the soup is ready." Elin, without missing a beat, took the chicken and stirred an invisible pot with it. The front row laughed. Then Kinsley and a boy from another class took the stage, and things went strange. The boy said, "Look, a spaceship is landing." Kinsley folded her arms and said, "No, that's not a spaceship, that's the gym ceiling, and you're not an astronaut, you're Kyle." The audience went quiet in a way that made the whole auditorium feel like a fridge. The boy stood there holding an offer nobody had taken, and the scene just stopped, like a video someone had paused.

Rosalie watched two more pairs. Whenever someone said no, that's not, the scene died in the same specific way, and whenever someone said yes, and, it moved. She began to suspect a pattern, like the vending machine outside the gym that only ate quarters. She could not see the rule itself, only its results, so she decided to test it. During her next scene with Elin, she planned to block on purpose, once, and see what happened.

They walked out. Elin said, "We're on a boat, Captain, there's a storm coming." The lights were hot on Rosalie's face and the rubber chicken was sweating in her hand. She said, "We're not on a boat. We're in the cafeteria, and it's taco day." Silence, except for one person coughing somewhere near the back. Elin's face went blank. Nothing came next, because there was no boat left to steer. Rosalie felt the scene land on the floor like a dropped tray, and she understood exactly what she had done. She had been the fridge.

"Blocking," whispered Kinsley from the side of the stage, sounding like she had finally found a word for the crime she herself had committed ten minutes earlier. Rosalie turned back to Elin, and this time she said, "Yes, and the storm just washed a seal onto the deck." Elin picked up the chicken, placed it on her head, and saluted it. The audience came back to life. "One seal aboard, Captain," she said, "and he outranks you."

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Scoring a line on thick card with a blunt tool before folding it gives a straight, clean fold instead of a cracked, bumpy one.
story:
Zachary spread the card across the kitchen table and pressed down the fold one more time, hoping it would look better. It didn't. The crease ran crooked and bumpy, and white cracks spidered through the blue paper where the fibers had torn instead of bending. His birthday card for his mom now looked like something a seagull had attacked.

"You're making another one?" Joshua asked, sliding into the chair across from him. Joshua had come over to work on his own card, a lopsided green thing with a dinosaur glued to the front. "That's your third."

"Fourth," Zachary said. He ran his thumb along the ruined fold. Something was wrong, and it wasn't the paper, because the first three sheets had all come from the same pack and cracked the same way. It wasn't the glue or the markers either. It was the fold itself. Thick card didn't want to bend, and when he forced it, it broke.

"Maybe she'll like the cracked look," Joshua offered. "Rustic."

"You're so pessimistic," Zachary said. Joshua shrugged and went back to his dinosaur. Zachary stared at the card, turning the problem over. He couldn't see why the card cracked, not really. It was something hidden inside the fold. But he could test ideas, the way he'd tested ideas in science class when the teacher couldn't just hand him the answer.

He picked up the dull end of a scissors, the side with no edge, and laid a ruler along where he wanted the fold to be. Then he dragged the blunt metal down the card in one slow line, pressing just hard enough to leave a shallow groove. The card felt different under his hand now, like it remembered where the fold belonged. He turned the card over and pushed the two halves together, and the fold went exactly along the scored line, sharp and clean, without a single crack.

"Whoa," Joshua said, leaning across the table. "Do that again."

Zachary did it again on a fresh piece, slower so Joshua could watch. "Scoring a line on thick card with a blunt tool before folding it gives you a straight, clean fold," he said. "Instead of a cracked, bumpy one." He held both cards up side by side, the ruined one and the scored one, and the difference was so obvious he almost laughed.

"I thought my cracks were fine," Joshua said. He looked down at his own card, then picked up the scissors and the ruler. "Actually, they're not. Give me that." He scored his fold, bent the card, and grinned at the crisp edge that appeared. "Okay, I was wrong. This is way better."

They worked until the light through the window began to fade and the glue smell had mostly evaporated from the tabletop. Zachary finished his mother's card, a dark blue one with a silver moon on the front, and folded it along the scored line one last time to make sure. It closed with a soft, clean snap.

"She's going to open it," Joshua said, "and the first thing she'll see is that perfect fold."

Zachary set the card against the sugar bowl and turned it until the moon faced them both.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: Demand for necessities, such as essential medicines, changes little when their price changes; economists call this inelastic demand.
story:
The peach stall at the farmers' market had a line twenty people long, and the sign read four dollars a basket, double last week's price. Benjamin stood beside his mother, who was there for the raw honey she used on his little sister's eczema, the kind the doctor had suggested when the creams stopped working. At the honey table, Mr. Johansson had raised his price too, from six dollars a jar to nine.

"Bad season for the bees," Mr. Johansson said. "Half my hives didn't make it through."

His mother bought two jars anyway, and so did the woman ahead of them, and the man behind them. Benjamin counted. In ten minutes, seven people bought honey at nine dollars. That didn't match what he'd seen at the peach stall, where people walked away when the line got long and the price got high, muttering that they'd come back for apples instead.

Rowyn was working the peach stall for her uncle, stacking baskets in the shade. "Everyone wants peaches this week," she said when Benjamin drifted over. "But half of them leave when they hear four dollars. My uncle says next week he'll drop it back to two and sell triple." She wanted the peaches to move fast because he paid her a bonus for every basket sold, and she was saving for a skate deck. Counting baskets all morning was tedious, she told him, but the bonus corresponded exactly to what she sold, one dollar for every ten.

Benjamin wandered back to the honey table and watched. Almost nobody left. One man winced at the price, then bought three jars anyway, saying his wife needed it for her allergies through the winter. Benjamin tried a simple test. He asked Mr. Johansson what would happen if the price went to twelve dollars.

"Same people would buy it," Mr. Johansson said. "Maybe one or two fewer. They need it. An old customer of mine, an economist type, called it inelastic demand. Necessities like medicine, they keep selling no matter what I charge." He shrugged. "Peaches aren't like that. Nobody needs a peach."

Jasper showed up at noon with his bike helmet under his arm, hunting for cheap plums for a smoothie stand he and Benjamin were planning. Between the peach stall and the honey table, they worked out the plan: buy the plentiful fruit cheap on Saturday, sell smoothies on Sunday when the crowds came. Jasper offered Benjamin a truce over their argument about who'd done more work last time, splitting the money straight down the middle, and Benjamin shook on it.

They bought plums at a dollar a basket from a farmer with a whole truckload and no line. Mr. Johansson waved as they passed, ringing up another jar of honey.

"Nine dollars," the customer said, counting out the bills, "and worth every one of them."

activity: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
knowledge_domain: to explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years through erosion and deposition
fact: A river cuts downward mainly because the sand, pebbles and boulders it carries grind against its bed, a process called abrasion.
story:
Everly sat on the back step of her grandpa's house with a shoebox of gravel, a glass jar, and a homework sheet that read, "Explain how a river carves a canyon over millions of years." She had one weekend. The creek behind the property was her only river, and it was about as radical as a bathtub, six inches deep and slow enough to count the leaves floating past.

She reached into the creek bed and pulled out a stone. It was gray and smooth, rounded like a small egg, with no sharp edges anywhere. Next to it lay a freshly broken chunk of the same kind of rock, all corners and points. Something had polished the smooth one. Water alone couldn't do that, she decided, because water was soft. It would be like trying to sand a table with a wet napkin.

She called her friend Davina, who arrived on a bike twenty minutes later with her phone out, ready to film whatever Everly was planning. "Watch," Everly said. She dropped two sharp-cornered chips of rock into the jar, added a handful of creek sand and some pebbles, filled it with water, and screwed on the lid. "Shake." They took turns shaking the jar for a long time, coordinating their efforts like a two-person crew, five minutes each, while Davina's little brother stood at the fence offering unhelpful commentary through a mouthful of crackers.

When they opened the jar, the water was cloudy with rock dust, and when Everly rubbed the chips between her fingers, the sharp edges felt dulled. Not smooth yet, but duller. "The river isn't just water," she said slowly. "It's water carrying sand, pebbles, boulders. All that stuff grinds against the bottom, and that's what cuts downward." Davina looked it up on her phone. "It's called abrasion," she reported. "There's your vocab word. You're welcome." Everly wrote it down, then added the rest: the grinding river scrapes its bed, deepens its channel a tiny bit at a stretch, and over millions of years that adds up to a canyon.

On Monday she stood up in Mr. Han's class with her jar, her dusty water, and her egg-smooth stone. "This rock was polished by the river itself," she said, holding it up. "Rivers are basically sandpaper that moves." Robert, in the second row, raised his hand. "So the Grand Canyon is just a very patient river with a lot of rocks?" Everly considered that. "Basically, yes." Mr. Han gave her project full marks and told her the jar of cloudy water had better not leak in anyone's backpack. Everly screwed the lid on twice.

activity: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
knowledge_domain: to explain how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War
fact: The treaty gave Poland a strip of land reaching the Baltic Sea, called the Polish Corridor, which cut East Prussia off from the rest of Germany.
story:
Landon spread the old atlas across his bedroom floor at nine o'clock at night, with his presentation due first period tomorrow. He had to explain to the class how the Treaty of Versailles helped lead to the Second World War, and so far all he had was a page of notes that said "Germany angry" three times in different handwriting. His mom had given him until ten, and the kitchen timer was already ticking.

He called Layla and Jasleen on video so they could collaborate, since they were stuck too. "Look at this map from before the war," Landon said, propping his phone above the atlas. "Germany's right here, all one big shape, but there's this weird bit floating off to the side, like an island, except it's not an island." He tapped the page. "A piece of Germany sitting all alone. That makes no sense."

Jasleen leaned closer to her camera. "Is it a printing error?" "It's in the legend," Layla said, squinting. "Maps don't just do that." Landon traced the shape with his finger and felt his stomach drop, because if it wasn't an error, then something had sliced Germany in two, and he had never once mentioned it in his notes. The timer in the kitchen ticked louder, or maybe it just seemed that way.

Then he found the thin line crossing the land between the two pieces, and the label beside it. "Poland," he read slowly. "The map calls it the Polish Corridor. Poland got a strip of land reaching the Baltic Sea." He followed the corridor with his fingernail, once, then again, making sure. "So that cut East Prussia off from the rest of Germany. That's why it looks like an island. It isn't one. It's stranded."

There was a silence on the call, then Jasleen said, "Write that down before you forget it." He did, in big letters at the top of the page, because suddenly the whole argument stood up in his mind like a row of dominoes: the treaty took land, people were furious about being split apart, and that anger fed the gradual slide into another war. "It's like a simile," Layla said. "Cutting a country in half and watching what it does next."

"What it does next is start the biggest war in history," Landon said. "Okay. I'm opening the presentation." He typed the first slide, deleted it, and typed a better one: a map with a red stripe through the middle of Germany, and a title that read, One Cut, Two Pieces, and the Corridor Between Them. The kitchen timer rang, and he hit save.

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: A claim can be checkable even if nobody has checked it yet; 'most students at our school walk to school' could be tested with a survey.
story:
The argument had followed Taylor home from school, buzzing in her ears like a trapped fly. Stefan had said it at lunch, flat and certain: "Most students at our school walk to school." Larissa had laughed and called it an opinion, the same thing she said about his opinions on cafeteria pizza. But Taylor wasn't so sure, and now she sat at the family computer with her chin on her fist, the keyboard warm under her fingers, thinking about the difference.

Her mom was a refugee who had come here with almost nothing, and she had a permanent habit of saying, "Don't argue about what you can count." She used to tell Taylor that her grandfather, a land surveyor, would inherit nothing to his daughter but his instruments and that one rule. Taylor had rolled her eyes at it for years. Tonight, though, the words circled back.

She opened a blank document and typed Stefan's sentence. Then, underneath it, she typed "Cafeteria pizza is gross." She stared at the two lines. The pizza one, nobody could ever settle; you'd just get opinions forever. But the walking one, that was different. You could ask every student how they got to school and count the answers. Nobody at her school had ever done that, she was fairly sure. It had never been checked. Even so, something told her it could be.

She messaged Larissa. "Stefan's thing about walking. Is it an opinion or what?"

"Opinion," Larissa typed back, fast as always. Then, a minute later: "wait."

Taylor grinned and kept typing. "We could check it. A survey. Ask everybody at school how they get here and count."

"Ms. Nur would let us do it at homeroom," Larissa replied. "I'll ask tomorrow if you make the sheet."

Taylor built the survey that night, four options and a line for name, the printer humming and the paper warm off the tray, smelling of ink. She imagined Stefan's face when the counts came in, and she imagined her own, because she realized she wanted him to be right and had no idea why.

The next afternoon she came home and found her mother at the computer, reading the survey sheet with her glasses low on her nose. "Most students at our school walk to school," her mother read aloud. "This is a claim that can be checked, even though no one has checked it yet." She looked up. "So. Are you going to be the one?"

Taylor took the stack of papers from the printer tray, squared the edges against the desk, and slid them into her backpack.

activity: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
knowledge_domain: to use a primary source like a settler's diary to explain why people moved west in the 1800s
fact: A settler's diary shows one person's view; it rarely tells how the Native American nations whose lands the trails crossed saw the same events.
story:
Parker sat at his grandmother's kitchen table with a shoebox of old papers between his elbows and a plate of warm cinnamon toast at his elbow, which was dangerous, because crumbs and hundred-year-old paper did not mix. His history objective for the weekend was to use a primary source, a document made by someone who was actually there, to explain why people moved west in the 1800s. His grandmother had gone straight to the closet and come back with the box. "My great-great-grandmother's diary," she said, tapping the cover like it was a door. "She walked part of the trail when she was hardly older than you."

The diary was smaller than Parker's hand, and the pages felt frail, like dry leaves that would crumble if he turned them too fast. The ink had faded to the color of weak tea. He read slowly, hunching so close that his nose almost touched the paper. "Land of our own," one entry said. "Papa says the soil in Oregon is black and deep as a loaf of bread." Another complained about oxen, rain, and boots with holes. Parker copied three quotes onto a note card and started to draft his paragraph right there, pencil scratching while the toast steamed.

Then he stopped. The diary told him why one family had gone west, sure. But the trail crossed land where people were already living, whole nations of people, and he turned every brittle page and found them only in the margins, if at all. One line mentioned "Indians" at a river crossing, and that was it. He sat back. The diary showed one person's view, he realized, like a keyhole. You could see through it, but only what was straight ahead. It almost never told how the Native American nations whose lands the trails crossed saw the very same events. That part of the story had walked another road entirely.

He tested the idea out loud, because that was how he thought best, and his grandmother was washing dishes anyway. "So if I only use this diary, my report has one eye." He held his hand over one eye like a patch. "Cheyenne's going to say I only looked from one side." His grandmother snorted into the dishwater. "Cheyenne says that about everything. She said it about my meatloaf." Parker texted Maliyah, who was doing the same assignment with an old letter from her attic. Her reply came fast: "Mine doesn't mention them either. We should say that in our reports. Mr. Nielsen keeps saying a source tells you what it tells you, not everything."

Parker opened his notebook and started a second draft, this time with a sentence at the end about the keyhole, about who was missing from the page and why the silence mattered. He worked until the light through the kitchen window turned gold, and the smell of cinnamon had faded into the smell of old paper. His grandmother set a fresh piece of toast beside him, farther from the diary this time. "Save room for the meatloaf," she said. "But maybe don't tell Cheyenne it exists."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Baking powder already contains both baking soda and a dry acid, so it can make batter rise without an acidic ingredient in the recipe.
story:
Willow had promised her family pancakes by ten o'clock, and by nine she was standing in the kitchen holding an empty tin that should have held baking powder. "How does it run out with no warning?" she muttered. The farmers' market opened at nine, so she grabbed her wallet and rode her bike down the hill to the row of white tents by the train station.

The air near the first stall emitted the smell of frying onions, strong enough to make her stomach growl even though pancakes were the mission. She passed a dilapidated old truck with peeling paint, its tailgate loaded with pumpkins, and found Mr. Francis at his table of honey, jam, and jars of pantry things. Beside him, Mike from her science class was stacking syrup bottles for his weekend job.

"I need baking powder," Willow said. "It's an emergency."

Mr. Francis shook his head. "Sold the last tin an hour ago. I've got baking soda, though." He held up a small box. Willow stared at it. Could you just swap one for the other? They both had "baking" in the name. But why would recipes ask for one sometimes and the other sometimes? That seemed like a clue, if she could figure out what it meant.

"Take the box," Mike said, "but think it through first." He pointed at a tin of baking powder a customer had left open on the table so people could smell the cornstarch. Willow picked it up and read the ingredient list. Baking soda was right there on the label, first or second. So baking powder contained baking soda, plus something else, something the box called an acid, in dry form. She turned the fact over in her mind. If the powder already had both parts inside it, then baking soda alone would be missing its partner. Her pancake recipe had no buttermilk, no yogurt, nothing sour. Nothing for the soda to work with.

"Wait," she said slowly. "The powder has the soda and the acid together, so it can rise the batter without anything acidic in the recipe. Plain soda can't do that, not in my recipe." Mike grinned and slid the box toward her anyway. "Or," he said, "you could add something sour. Mr. Francis sells lemon juice."

She bought the soda and a small lemon, and back home she squeezed half of it into the batter and watched. The surface fizzed and bubbled, tiny eruptions all across the top, and when the first pancake hit the hot pan it rose fat and golden. Willow leaned close, listening to it sputter, and flipped it high toward the ceiling. "Perfect catch," said her little brother, mouth already open.

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: Bones show up white on an X-ray because the calcium in them absorbs more X-rays than the softer tissue around them.
story:
The waiting room of Riverside Medical had one wall of windows, a fish tank, and a sign that asked, "Is your cough contagious? Please wear a mask." Bennett sat under the sign with his left arm wrapped in a sling, holding a wrinkled X-ray the technician had printed for him after the second round of pictures. He had fallen off the church parking lot wall on Tuesday, and today, in exactly twelve minutes, the doctor would put the cast on. Once the cast was on, it would be six weeks before he could do anything about the bet.

The bet was with Joelle. She had texted him a photo of her own X-ray from her cousin's file last month, and she insisted the machine "lit the bones up like a flashlight." Bennett had said no way, the bones had to already look different to the machine somehow, and whoever was right had to distribute his leftover Halloween candy to the loser, all of it, even the peanut butter cups. He had until Friday. He had, more urgently, about twelve minutes of sitting in this exact hallway where the X-ray room was.

He stared at the film. His forearm bones glowed white. His skin was a gray shadow you could barely see, more of a smudge than a shape. If the machine lit things up, why not the skin? It was closer to the machine. He turned the film sideways, then held it up against the window light. The bones stayed white no matter what. So the difference was in the bones themselves, not the light. Something they were made of.

On the wall across from him hung a poster of a glass of milk with the words STRONG BONES above it, and under that, the word calcium. Bennett chewed on that. His mom made him drink milk because calcium built bones. So bones were full of calcium, and calcium was hard stuff, dense stuff. Maybe dense stuff soaked up the X-ray beam the way a thick towel soaks up water, and whatever soaked up the beam came out white on the film. Soft stuff let the beam pass straight through, so it barely showed at all. He needed to test it.

There was a bowl of chalky antacid tablets at the front desk. The label listed calcium as the main ingredient. Bennett asked the technician, who was pushing a cart past, "Can I borrow one tablet and thirty seconds on your machine before the doctor comes?" She looked at his sling, then at the clock, and shrugged. He set the tablet on the film holder where his arm had been, and the tech ran the beam for a breath. The picture showed a small white square, bright as his bones, sitting in nothing.

Joelle was in the waiting room, having been dropped off with Shannon after school to sign his cast early. Bennett held up both films side by side, the arm and the tablet. Joelle leaned in, then stood up straight and let out a groan. "Fine. Calcium. Bones are white because the calcium in them absorbs more X-rays than the softer stuff around them." She dug the peanut butter cups out of her backpack and set them on his knee. The doctor came through the door with a bucket of green casting tape and said, "Who's ready for the Bennett dynasty's fifth broken bone?"

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During Mexico's Dia de los Muertos on November 1 and 2, families build altars called ofrendas with photos and marigolds, whose color and scent are said to guide spirits home.
story:
Chloe sat in the back seat of the family car with a shoebox on her lap, and inside the shoebox was a photograph of her grandfather, taken the summer before he died. Her mother was driving across town to Mr. Guo's house, where the whole neighborhood was building an altar for the first of November. Chloe had promised to bring the photo, but now that the box was open on her knees, she couldn't make herself take it out. The plan was to set the picture among the marigolds so the color and the scent could guide him home. That was the whole point. And if it worked, if he actually came, what then?

"I still don't get how flowers lead anybody anywhere," said Franklin, who was squeezed in beside her with a paper bag of marigold petals he had picked from his aunt's garden. He had wanted to come, though he pretended it was only because his aunt had too many marigolds and would otherwise demolish the whole bed to plant tulips. "Like, is there a rule? Does the smell wear off halfway?"

"It's not arbitrary," Chloe said. "The color and the scent are supposed to point the way home. Two days, November first and second. If there's a rule, I can test it." She had been turning an idea over since breakfast: if the marigolds made a path, then a broken path might not work, and a longer one might work better. She could scatter the petals in a line straight toward the photo and see whether anything felt different, whether the air in the room shifted, whether her mother's shoulders dropped.

At Mr. Guo's house, the altar stood against the living room wall, three shelves deep with candles and bread and little sugar skulls. "We call it an ofrenda," Mr. Guo said, moving a candle two inches to the left, like a man who had done this many times and knew exactly where things belonged. He wanted the altar finished before sunset, because his own mother's photo was coming by mail and he needed the shelf ready. That was his want, and he was not going to let anyone dawdle.

Chloe placed her grandfather's photograph on the second shelf. Franklin opened his bag of petals, and together they scattered them in a line across the rug, a golden path from the front door to the ofrenda. Some petals bounced off Mr. Guo's shoe; he brushed them straight without a word. The room filled with a sharp, sweet smell, brighter than the candles. Nothing happened that Chloe could name. Her mother stood looking at the photo, and after a while she laughed at something in his face in the picture, that crooked grin, and wiped her eyes with the back of her hand.

"Did it work?" Franklin whispered.

Chloe looked at the path of petals, the picture, her mother laughing. "The petals go all the way to the door," she said. "He'd have to be pretty lost to miss it." Then she straightened the frame so it faced the doorway, dead center of the marigolds.
